assignments.title: 🪨 A Rock’s Journey: Shaping Earth Over Time
assignments.html:
🪨 A Rock’s Journey: Shaping Earth Over Time

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.6.1– Describe and give examples of ways in which Earth’s surface is built up and torn down by physical and chemical weathering, erosion, and deposition.

🎯 Objective:

Independently create a short narrative told from a rock’s point of view, giving the rock a name, personality, and voice, while demonstrating understanding of how weathering, erosion, and deposition change Earth’s surface over time.

🌌 Mission Briefing:

Welcome, Geological Storytellers.

 

Earth’s surface is never still. Rocks crack, crumble, travel, and settle as natural processes reshape the planet over time. Your mission is to become a rock and tell your life story as Earth changes you.

 

You will give your rock a name, a personality, and a voice, then explain how weathering breaks you down, erosion moves you, and deposition determines where you end up.

 

Your story should sound like the rock is alive, observant, and experiencing its journey through Earth’s systems—while still using accurate science. 🌍🪨

🧰 Steps:

1️⃣ Write A Rock’s Story

Write a short story from the rock’s point of view.

 

📝 Writing Requirements:

  • At least 3 paragraphs

  • Each paragraph must be 4–6 complete sentences

  • Written in first person (I, me, my)

  • Your rock must have:

    • A name

    • A personality (brave, grumpy, curious, patient, adventurous, etc.)

    • A clear story that follows its journey over time

🧪 Science Requirements (MUST Be Included in the Story)

🪨 Weathering

  • Clearly identify the type of weathering that breaks you down

    • Physical (ice wedging, plant roots, abrasion)

    • Chemical (acid rain, oxidation, dissolution)

 

🌊 Erosion

  • Clearly identify the force of erosion that moves you

    • Water

    • Wind

    • Ice (glaciers)

    • Gravity

 

🏖️ Deposition

  • Clearly describe where you are deposited

    • River delta

    • Beach

    • Desert dune

    • Ocean floor

    • Valley

📚 Vocabulary

Correctly use at least 5 of the following terms in your story and underline each vocabulary word when it appears.

  • Weathering

  • Erosion

  • Deposition

  • Sediment

  • Gravity

  • Glacier

  • Acid rain

  • Abrasion

  • Delta

 

👉 Reminder: If a vocabulary word is not underlined, it will not count toward your total—even if it is used correctly.

✍️ Writing Format Options

You may choose ONE of the following ways to complete and submit your story:

 

📝 Option 1: Handwritten (Science Notebook)

  • Write your story neatly in your science notebook

  • Take a clear, well-lit photo of your work

  • All writing must be easy to read

  • Make sure underlined vocabulary words are clearly visible

 

📸 If your photo is blurry or hard to read, it will be returned for resubmission.

💻 Option 2: Typed (Digital Submission)

  • Type your story in a Word document or Google Doc

  • Use proper paragraphs and complete sentences

  • Underline all vocabulary words in the document

  • Attach the file directly to the assignment

2️⃣ Design a Cover Image Using AI

After writing your story, use AI to design a cover image for your rock’s story.

 

🎨 Your Cover Image Must Include:

  • Your rock (matching its personality)

  • At least one Earth process (weathering, erosion, or deposition)

    • Try including a scene from your story!

  • A title for your story

🧠 AI Prompt Example (You MUST Create Your Own)

Your AI prompt could look something like this, but it must match your story.

Your AI prompt should match your story and may be in any art style (cartoon, anime, realistic, illustrated, etc.). Remember to be specific. Describe your story and what you chose to write.

 

Example Prompt:

“A children’s book cover showing a named rock with a personality traveling through nature as it is weathered, eroded, and deposited. The rock is expressive and tells its own story. The scene includes rivers, mountains, beaches, or glaciers. Colorful and educational.”

📝 Assignment Submission

Submit the following:

📄 1. Your Written Story
A complete 3+ paragraph story written from the rock’s point of view, including a name, personality, accurate science, and underlined vocabulary words.

 

🖼️ 2. AI-Generated Cover Image
A clear, creative image that represents your rock’s journey and personality.

📊 Rubric 

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 10 Clearly and accurately explains weathering, erosion, and deposition aligned to SC.6.E.6.1
📚 Vocabulary Use 5 Correctly uses at least 5 required vocabulary terms and underlines them
✍️ Storytelling & Point of View 10 Story is written from the rock’s point of view and includes a name, personality, voice, and clear storyline
🎨 AI Cover Image 5 Image matches the rock’s story, personality, and Earth process

💯 This assignment is worth 30 points total.

assignments.title: 🏞️ Earth’s Landforms: A VR Field Report
assignments.html:
🏞️ Earth’s Landforms: A VR Field Report

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.6.2 – Recognize that there are a variety of different landforms on Earth’s surface such as coastlines, dunes, rivers, mountains, glaciers, deltas, and lakes and relate these landforms as they apply to Florida.

🎯 Objective

Independently create a VR video report explaining how a specific landform forms and changes over time.

 

Students will demonstrate understanding of landforms, erosion, deposition, and Earth-shaping forces through accurate science explanations, correct vocabulary usage, and verbal communication in VR.

🌌 Mission Briefing

Earth’s surface may look stable, but it is constantly changing.

 

Wind moves sand across deserts and beaches.
Water erodes rock and carries sediment downstream.
Ice slowly scrapes and carves the land beneath it.

 

Over thousands to millions of years, these forces shape Earth’s surface into the landforms we see today.

 

Scientists study landforms to understand:

  • How Earth has changed in the past

  • What forces are shaping it right now

  • How landscapes may continue to change in the future

 

Your mission is to step into virtual reality as a field scientist and report on one landform. You will explain what it is, how it formed, what force shapes it most, and how it continues to change over time.

 

Your goal is not just to name a landform, but to explain the processes behind it — showing that Earth’s surface is active, dynamic, and always evolving. 🌍

🧰 Step 1: Choose Your Landform

Choose ONE landform to investigate:

  • 🌊 Coastline

  • 🏜️ Dune

  • 🏞️ River

  • 🏔️ Mountain

  • ❄️ Glacier

  • 🌊 Delta

  • 💧 Lake

🎥 Step 2: VR Video Report Requirements

Record a 60–90 second VR video report explaining your chosen landform.

 

Your video should clearly walk through each step below.
Think of this as a spoken science explanation, not a script you read word-for-word.

1️⃣ What the landform is

Clearly name your landform and describe what kind of natural feature it is.

 

Explain:

  • What the landform looks like

  • Where it is found on Earth

  • How it is different from other landforms

2️⃣ How the landform forms

Explain how the landform is created.

 

Describe:

  • What materials are involved (rock, sand, sediment, ice, water)

  • What processes cause it to form

  • Whether it forms slowly or quickly

 

Use cause-and-effect language such as:
because, as a result, over time, when…then…

3️⃣ Which force shapes it most

Identify the main force responsible for shaping your landform.

 

Choose ONE:

  • Water

  • Wind

  • Ice

  • Gravity

 

Explain:

  • How this force moves material

  • How it causes erosion or deposition

  • Why this force matters more than others for your landform

4️⃣ How the landform changes over time

Explain how the landform is not permanent.

 

Describe:

  • How erosion wears it down

  • How deposition builds it up

  • How its shape or size changes over long periods of time

 

Be sure to emphasize:

  • These changes take thousands to millions of years

📚 Step 3: Required Vocabulary

You must correctly use at least 5 vocabulary words from the list that matches your chosen landform.

 

👉 Vocabulary only counts if it is used correctly and in context during your video.

🌊 Coastline Vocabulary

  • Coastline

  • Erosion

  • Waves

  • Sediment

  • Deposition

  • Barrier island

  • Shoreline

🏜️ Dune Vocabulary

  • Dune

  • Wind

  • Sand

  • Erosion

  • Deposition

  • Sediment

  • Movement

🏞️ River Vocabulary

  • River

  • Flow

  • Erosion

  • Sediment

  • Deposition

  • Channel

  • Freshwater

🏔️ Mountain Vocabulary

  • Mountain

  • Elevation

  • Tectonic plates

  • Volcano

  • Uplift

  • Erosion

  • Peak

❄️ Glacier Vocabulary

  • Glacier

  • Ice

  • Movement

  • Erosion

  • Valley

  • Climate

  • Ice sheet

  • Sediment

🌊 Delta Vocabulary

  • Delta

  • Sediment

  • Deposition

  • River mouth

  • Flow

  • Fan-shaped

  • Landform

💧 Lake Vocabulary

  • Lake

  • Freshwater

  • Basin

  • Runoff

  • Sediment

  • Glacier

  • Shore

  • Erosion

⭐ Bonus Opportunity: Real-World Landform Spotlight (+2 points)

Students may earn up to 2 bonus points by going deeper with their real-world example.

 

To earn bonus points:

  • Describe a specific real-world location where your landform exists

  • Explain why this location is a strong example of your landform

  • Clearly connect Earth’s forces (water, wind, ice, or gravity) to how the landform formed or is changing there

 

This bonus is optional and will not affect your base score.

🧠 Important Reminder

Every report must clearly show that:

  • Landforms are natural

  • They form over long periods of time

  • Earth’s surface is shaped by water, wind, ice, or gravity

🎮 Step 4: VR Environment

Choose a VR environment that best represents your landform.

 

The environment does not need to be perfect — your explanation matters more than realism.

 

You may:

  • Point to features

  • Gesture while explaining

  • Move around the environment as you present

📝 Step 5: Assignment Submission

Submit ALL of the following:

🎥 1. VR Video Report (2D Video Only)
A clear, complete explanation that meets all science and vocabulary requirements.

 

⚠️ Important Reminder:
Your submission must be a 2D video recording, not a spatial recording.

💡 Quick Tip (Read Before Submitting)

If you accidentally record a spatial recording and need to resubmit:

  • Load your spatial recording

  • Play it back

  • Then take a 2D video of your recording while it plays

 

This allows you to submit the correct format without re-recording your entire presentation.

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 10 Correct explanation of landform formation and Earth-shaping forces
📚 Vocabulary Use 5 At least 5 landform-specific terms used correctly
🎤 Clarity & Explanation 10 Clear, organized, science-based verbal explanation
🎮 VR Engagement 5 On-task use of VR environment
Total 30 points

 

⭐ Bonus: +2 points for a detailed, accurate real-world landform example.

💯 This assignment is worth 30 points total, with up to 2 bonus points available.

📰 OPTIMA Times: Florida’s Landforms Special Issue

Breaking News: Florida’s Surface Is Changing — and You’re Reporting the Story!

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.6.2 – Recognize that there are a variety of different landforms on Earth’s surface such as coastlines, dunes, rivers, mountains, glaciers, deltas, and lakes and relate these landforms as they apply to Florida.

🎯 Objective

Use AI tools and Canva to design a science magazine cover for The OPTIMA Times that explains one Florida landform and how it forms or changes over time.

 

Your mission: report on Florida’s surface like a science journalist, combining accurate science with clear visuals and headlines.

💬 Essential Question

“How do Florida’s landforms form and change — and how can scientists explain them to the public?”

🧠 Mission Briefing

Breaking news from the Sunshine State, Science Correspondent! 🌴

 

Florida’s land may look calm and flat, but powerful forces are always at work. Water, wind, weather, and erosion slowly reshape Florida’s surface every day.

 

Unlike many states, Florida does not have mountains or glaciers. Instead, Florida’s landforms include:

  • Coastlines reshaped by waves and storms

  • Dunes built and moved by wind

  • Slow-moving rivers that flood easily

  • Lakes formed by low elevation and sinkholes

  • Estuaries where freshwater and saltwater mix

 

Your assignment is to investigate one Florida landform and report on it for a special issue of The OPTIMA Times.

 

To deepen your understanding, you must choose a different landform than the one you reported on last week. This ensures you are exploring new science, not repeating the same example.

🧩 Assignment Steps

1️⃣ Choose Your Florida Landform

Select ONE Florida landform that is different from the landform you reported on last week:

🌊 Coastline
🏜️ Dune
🏞️ River
💧 Lake
🌊 Estuary

 

❌ Mountains and glaciers may NOT be chosen because they do not exist in Florida.

2️⃣ Generate Your Visual

Use an AI image generator to create an image of your chosen Florida landform.

 

Your image must:

  • Clearly show the landform

  • Represent Florida specifically

  • Leave space for headlines and text

 

This image will become the main cover photo for your magazine.

3️⃣ Design Your Magazine Cover in Canva

Go to Canva and search for magazine cover template.

 

Choose a layout that fits a science or nature magazine.

 

Your cover must include:

  • 📰 Magazine Title: OPTIMA Times

  • 🗞️ Main Headline related to your landform

  • 📝 A supporting headline and blurbs

  • 🖼️ Your AI-generated image as the background

 

Your final product should look like a real magazine cover, not a poster or slideshow. 

Take a look at my example Magazine cover about Florida Coastlines.

🧠 Important Reminder

Your creativity may vary — but the science expectations do not.

 

Every magazine cover must clearly show that:

  • Florida is flat and low in elevation

  • Water is the main force shaping Florida’s land

  • Florida does not have mountains or glaciers

  • The chosen landform is explained accurately

📤 Submit Your Work

Submit the of the following:

🖼️ 1. Final Magazine Cover Image
Downloaded as a PNG or JPG (no links).

 

⚠️ Links will not be accepted. Files must be uploaded to receive full credit.

📊 Rubric 

Category Points Description
🧪 Science Accuracy 5 Landform is explained correctly and applies to Florida
📰 Magazine Design 5 Layout is clear, organized, and magazine-style
Total 10 points

 

💯 This assignment is worth 10 points total.

🏞️ Earth’s Landforms: 3D Pen Surface Features Model
A Hands-On Earth Science Construction Challenge

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.6.2 – Recognize that there are a variety of different landforms on Earth’s surface such as coastlines, dunes, rivers, mountains, glaciers, deltas, and lakes and relate these landforms as they apply to Florida.

🎯 Objective
Create a physical 3D pen drawing that demonstrates your understanding of Earth’s landforms by showing how natural features form and exist on Earth’s surface.

 

You will choose ONE landform and build a 3D Pen Drawing that shows:

• What the landform looks like
• Where it is found
• How it exists on Earth’s surface

💬 Essential Question
What are landforms, and how do they shape the surface of Earth?

🧠 Mission Briefing

Earth’s surface is not flat, plain, or boring.

 

It is covered in landforms — natural features that were not built by humans and that formed over long periods of timedue to:

• Water
• Wind
• Ice
• Gravity

 

Some landforms are tall and massive.
Some are wide and flat.
Some are carved by rivers.
Some are built by ice or sand.

 

Your mission is to choose ONE landform and build a 3D pen drawing of it using the 3D pen to prove that you understand what it is and how it exists on Earth.

🧩 Assignment Task:

You must create a 3D pen model of ONE of the following landforms:

 

Choose ONE:

• 🌊 Coastline
• 🏜️ Dune
• 🏞️ River
• 🏔️ Mountain
• ❄️ Glacier
• 🌊 Delta
• 💧 Lake

 

Your model must:

✅ Be drawn with your 3D pen in VR
✅ Clearly show the shape of the landform
✅ Be clearly labeled
✅ Be made ONLY with a 3D pen (NO IFX)

 

🧠 Make sure your model shows:

• The name of the landform
• The main features of the landform
• The surface it sits on (land or water)

🛑 CRITICAL RULES (READ CAREFULLY)

❌ NO IFX
✅ ONLY 3D PEN CREATIONS FROM ENGAGE WILL BE ACCEPTED

 

If it has IFX in any way → It will receive a ZERO.

💡 If You Missed Class or Choose Not to Enter VR:

If you were absent or did not complete the VR experience during class time, you MUST log into the afterschool session to complete this assignment. You can find the afterschool session code is posted in our Canvas Announcements page.

 

➡️ This is now a REQUIRED GRADED HOMEWORK ASSIGNMENT
➡️ This counts as a QUIZ GRADE

📸 Submission:

Submit:

🖼️ 1 Image of your 3D pen model from VR during class

 

Your image must:

• Clearly show the plastic 3D pen lines
• Clearly show the entire landform
• Clearly show labels

📊 Rubric

Category Points Description

🎯 Objective

🌌 Mission Briefing

At first glance, Earth looks calm and peaceful.

But in reality, our planet is under constant attack.

 

Every day, Earth is bombarded by:

  • ☄️ Meteors racing through space

  • ☀️ Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun

  • 🌡️ Extreme hot and cold temperatures

 

And yet… Earth remains the perfect home for life.

Why?

 

Because Earth has a powerful, invisible protector.

The atmosphere.

 

The atmosphere is an invisible shield made of gases and arranged in layers. It works nonstop to:

  • Block harmful radiation

  • Burn up meteors before they hit the ground

  • Trap heat so the planet stays warm enough for life


Without it, Earth would be frozen, burned, and lifeless.

 

Your mission is to tell the story of the day the atmosphere saved Earth using a science comic book.

🎯 Objective

In this mission, you will take on the role of a field scientist exploring how Earth is organized into five major spheres. As you investigate your environment—whether inside your home, in your backyard, or in your neighborhood—you will look closely at the world around you to identify real-life examples of each sphere.

  • Observe and record examples of the geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere

  • Classify each example accurately

By completing this mission, you will strengthen your observation skills, build scientific reasoning, and develop a deeper understanding of how Earth’s systems shape the planet we live on.

🌎 Mission Briefing

Earth may look simple on the surface, but it is actually made of five powerful systems that work together every moment to shape our planet:

  • 🪨 Geosphere — solid Earth

  • 🌊 Hydrosphere — liquid water

  • ❄️ Cryosphere — frozen water

  • 🌬️ Atmosphere — gases

None of these spheres works alone. They constantly interact:

  • Water shapes and erodes land

  • Air affects weather and temperature

  • Living things depend on air, water, and land

These systems are like players on a team: each has a job, and all contribute to keeping Earth functioning.

💬 Essential Question
How do Earth’s spheres help us understand how Earth works as a system?

🧠 Mission Briefing

Earth is made up of several large systems called spheres. Each sphere includes different parts of Earth and has a specific role. While the spheres work together, each one can be studied on its own to better understand Earth.

 

There are five major Earth spheres:

• Geosphere – solid land
• Hydrosphere – liquid water
• Cryosphere – frozen water
• Atmosphere – air
• Biosphere – living things

Geosphere (Solid Earth)
Includes all solid, non-living parts of Earth.

Examples may include rocks, soil, sand, mountains, cliffs, or landforms.

Do not include water, ice, air, or living things.

Hydrosphere (Liquid Water)
Includes all liquid water on Earth.

Examples may include oceans, rivers, lakes, rain, or groundwater.

Do not include ice or snow.

Cryosphere (Frozen Water)
Includes all frozen water on Earth.

Examples may include glaciers, ice caps, snow, or ice sheets.

Do not include liquid water.

Atmosphere (Air)
The layer of gases surrounding Earth.

Examples may include air, clouds, wind, or gases such as oxygen or nitrogen.

Do not focus on solid land or living organisms.

Biosphere (Living Things)
Includes all living organisms.

Examples may include plants, animals, humans, trees, or microorganisms.

Living things may interact with other spheres, but your focus should remain on life.

🥼 Demonstration Station: Earth’s Spheres & Their Interactions

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.7.4– Describe how the interactions of the geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere affect the Earth.

🎯 Objective
Independently create a demonstration scene that shows how two or more of Earth’s spheres interact and affect one another.

 

Through this task, scholars will model Earth as a connected system, using visual evidence to show how matter and energy move between spheres. Students will demonstrate their understanding by building, labeling, and explainingsphere interactions using in-world sticky notes rather than written paragraphs.

 

This assignment is designed to help students move beyond identifying Earth’s spheres and instead focus on cause-and-effect relationships between systems. By the end of this activity, students should be able to clearly show that a change in one sphere can lead to changes in another, reinforcing the idea that Earth’s systems are interdependent and constantly interacting.

🌌 Mission Briefing
Earth may look like it is made of separate parts, but it operates as one connected system.

 

Water shapes land.
Air moves moisture and energy.
Ice melts and changes water systems.
Living things interact with air, land, and water.

 

These parts of Earth — called spheres — constantly interact by exchanging matter and energy.

 

A change in one sphere can cause changes in others, shaping Earth and supporting life.

 

Scientists study these interactions to understand:

  • How Earth’s surface changes over time

  • How ecosystems are supported

  • How natural events like floods, storms, erosion, and melting ice affect the planet

 

Your mission is to step into virtual reality as a systems scientist and enter the Demonstration Station.

 

You will build, label, and explain how Earth’s spheres interact using a visual model and in-world sticky notes.

 

Your goal is not just to identify the spheres, but to prove the interaction — showing clear cause and effect and demonstrating that Earth works as one connected system. 🌍

🧰 Step 1: Choose Your Sphere Interaction
Choose ONE Earth-sphere interaction to demonstrate.

You may use any example below or design your own scientifically accurate interaction.

🌊 Hydrosphere ↔ Geosphere

Water interacts with land and rock.

 

Examples:

  • Rain causing erosion on a hillside

  • Rivers carving valleys

  • Waves wearing away coastlines

  • Sediment being deposited to form deltas

  • Flooding changing land shape

  • Groundwater wearing away rock

🌬️ Atmosphere ↔ Hydrosphere

Air and water interact in the water cycle.

 

Examples:

  • Water evaporating from oceans, lakes, or rivers

  • Cloud formation

  • Rain or snow falling

  • Wind moving clouds

  • Storm systems forming over warm water

🌱 Biosphere ↔ Atmosphere

Living things depend on and change the air.

 

Examples:

  • Plants taking in carbon dioxide

  • Plants releasing oxygen

  • Animals breathing oxygen

  • Forests affecting air quality

  • Vegetation influencing local climate

❄️ Cryosphere ↔ Hydrosphere

Frozen and liquid water interact.

 

Examples:

  • Glaciers melting into rivers

  • Snow melting into lakes

  • Icebergs melting in the ocean

  • Seasonal snowpack feeding rivers

  • Melting ice affecting sea levels

🌱 Biosphere ↔ Geosphere

Living things interact with land.

 

Examples:

  • Plant roots breaking rock

  • Trees growing in soil

  • Animals burrowing

  • Humans changing land surfaces

  • Vegetation preventing erosion

🌬️ Atmosphere ↔ Geosphere

Air affects land directly.

 

Examples:

  • Wind erosion in deserts

  • Sand dunes forming

  • Dust storms reshaping land

  • Temperature changes cracking rocks

🌊 Hydrosphere ↔ Biosphere

Water supports life.

 

Examples:

  • Plants growing near rivers

  • Animals drinking from lakes

  • Fish living in oceans

  • Wetlands supporting ecosystems

  • Water availability affecting habitats

🌀 Multi-Sphere Interactions

Some interactions involve more than two spheres.

 

Examples:

  • Rain (atmosphere) erodes land (geosphere) and supports plants (biosphere)

  • Melting glaciers (cryosphere) increase river flow (hydrosphere) and change habitats (biosphere)

  • Storms (atmosphere) cause flooding (hydrosphere) that reshapes land (geosphere)

🎮 Step 2: Demonstration Scene Requirements
Build a scene that clearly shows how your chosen spheres interact.

Your demonstration must include ALL of the following:

🏷️ Sticky Note Labels

  • At least TWO sticky notes that:

    • Clearly label each Earth sphere

    • Explain what each sphere is or does

🔄 Sticky Notes for Interactions

  • Additional sticky notes that:

    • Explain how the spheres interact

    • Describe what is moving (water, air, ice, organisms, sediment)

    • Show clear cause and effect between spheres

 

Sticky notes should be placed directly next to the part of the scene they explain.

 

👉 Tip: Using science vocabulary (such as interaction, system, matter, energy, erosion, evaporation, deposition) will help make your explanations clearer and stronger.

🧠 Important Reminder
Your demonstration must show that:

  • Earth’s spheres interact

  • Matter or energy moves between systems

  • A change in one sphere can affect others

  • Earth works as one connected system

🎮 Step 3: Environment Choice
Choose an environment that best represents your interaction.

 

The environment does not need to be perfect —
your model and explanations matter more than realism.

 

You may move objects, adjust terrain, and place sticky notes where they make the interaction clear.

📝 Step 4: Assignment Submission
Submit as many images as you need to clearly show your work.

 

Your images must clearly show:

  • At least two Earth spheres

  • The information written on your sticky notes

🎯 Objective
Independly create an infographic-style poster that visually explains how heat energy moves through one type of heat transfer: radiation, conduction, or convection.

 

Through this task, you will communicate scientific ideas using diagrams, layout, color, and concise explanations rather than long written responses. Scientists often use visuals to explain complex ideas, and this assignment focuses on building those same science communication skills.

 

This assignment is designed to move you beyond memorizing definitions and toward understanding how heat transfer actually works in real-world situations. By the end of this activity, you should be able to clearly show how energy moves from warmer areas to cooler areas and explain why your chosen type of heat transfer occurs.

🌌 Mission Briefing
Heat energy is constantly moving all around us, even when we do not notice it.

 

It warms Earth from the Sun, moves through the air and oceans, heats buildings, cooks food, and affects weather patterns. Understanding how heat moves helps scientists explain climate, engineering, technology, and everyday experiences.

 

Scientists describe three main types of heat transfer:

Radiation — heat transfer through electromagnetic waves
Conduction — heat transfer through direct contact
Convection — heat transfer through movement of fluids like air or water

 

Each type works differently, but all follow the same basic rule: heat moves from warmer areas to cooler areas.

 

Your mission is to enter the Thermal Transfer Studio and design an educational infographic poster that clearly explains ONE type of heat transfer.

 

Your goal is not just to name the type, but to visually show how heat moves, where it happens in real life, and why understanding heat transfer matters in science and everyday life.

☀️ Radiation — Heat Transfer Through Waves
Radiation transfers heat through electromagnetic waves and does not require direct contact or a material medium.

 

You might include:

• Heat from the Sun warming Earth
• Feeling warmth from a fire or heater without touching it
• Heat from a light bulb
• Heat absorbed by pavement or sand
• Solar panels absorbing energy
• Infrared heat lamps

 

Helpful visuals could show heat waves traveling through space or air.

🪵 Conduction — Heat Transfer Through Direct Contact
Conduction occurs when heat transfers between objects that are touching. It works especially well in solids, particularly metals.

 

You might include:

• A metal spoon heating up in hot soup
• Walking barefoot on hot pavement
• Holding a warm mug or ice cube
• A pan heating food on a stove
• Ice melting in your hand
• Heat moving through walls, desks, or countertops

 

Helpful visuals could show particles vibrating and transferring energy through contact.

 

This option works well if you like hands-on examples, cooking, or everyday physical interactions.

🌬️ Convection — Heat Transfer Through Fluid Movement
Convection happens when heat moves through liquids or gases. Warm fluid rises, and cooler fluid sinks, creating circulating currents.

 

You might include:

• Boiling water in a pot
• Hot air rising from a heater
• Ocean currents moving warm and cool water
• Wind patterns or weather systems
• Lava movement beneath Earth’s crust
• Air circulation in rooms or buildings

 

Helpful visuals could show circular motion or convection currents.

 

This option works well if you like weather, oceans, Earth science, or large-scale systems.

💧 The Journey of a Water Drop: A Deep Dive Into the Water Cycle

 

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.7.2 – Investigate and apply how the cycling of water between the atmosphere and hydrosphere has an effect on weather patterns and climate.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will build a 360° VR model of the water cycle to show how water moves through Earth’s system.

 

Water on Earth is always moving. The water in oceans, rivers, lakes, plants, clouds, and even underground is part of one connected system. Water constantly travels between the hydrosphere (Earth’s water) and the atmosphere (the air around Earth).

 

As water moves through this system, it may change form. It can exist as liquid water, water vapor (gas), or ice. The movement of water through these changes is called the water cycle.

 

The Sun provides the energy that keeps the water cycle moving. When sunlight warms water at Earth’s surface, evaporation begins. Water vapor rises into the atmosphere, forms clouds, and eventually falls back to Earth as precipitation. From there, the water may collect, flow downhill, soak into the ground, or return to plants.

 

The continuous cycling of water also plays an important role in weather and climate, because water in the atmosphere forms clouds and precipitation that influence weather patterns around the world.

 

Using a 360° IFX environment, you will create a model that shows how water travels through this continuous cycle.

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

Explain how water moves between the hydrosphere and atmosphere

Identify the stages of the water cycle

Describe how the Sun powers the cycle

Explain how the water cycle influences weather

🌌 Mission Briefing

Imagine you are following one drop of water.

 

This drop might begin in the ocean, a lake, a river, or even moisture in the soil. When the Sun warms the water, the drop gains energy and changes into water vapor through evaporation. It rises into the atmosphere where the air is cooler.

 

As the water vapor cools, it forms tiny droplets and becomes part of a cloud. This process is called condensation.

 

Eventually, the droplets in the cloud become too heavy and fall back to Earth as precipitation.

 

Once the water returns to Earth, several things can happen. It may collect in lakes or oceans, flow downhill across land as runoff, soak into the ground through infiltration, or move into plants and return to the atmosphere through transpiration.

 

Then the cycle begins again.

 

This continuous cycling of water helps form clouds, storms, and precipitation, which influence weather patterns and climate on Earth.

Your mission is to tell the story of this journey inside a 360° VR environment. Someone exploring your world should be able to look around and follow the path of water through the entire cycle.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will create a VR breaking news broadcast explaining how the water cycle leads to the formation of rainstorms.

 

Water is constantly moving between Earth’s surface and the atmosphere through processes such as evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. These processes make up the water cycle, which moves both water and energy throughout Earth’s system.

 

When the Sun heats water on Earth’s surface, liquid water changes into water vapor through evaporation. This water vapor rises into the atmosphere and increases the humidity, or the amount of water vapor in the air.

As warm, moist air rises higher in the atmosphere, it begins to cool. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor, so the vapor changes into tiny droplets of liquid water through condensation. These droplets gather together to form clouds.

When droplets in clouds collide and grow larger, they eventually become too heavy to remain in the air and fall back to Earth as precipitation, such as rain.

These same processes can lead to the development of rainstorms, especially when large amounts of warm, moist air rise quickly into the atmosphere.

 

In this assignment, you will act as a news reporter inside a VR news studio and produce a short breaking news bulletinexplaining how the stages of the water cycle lead to the formation of a rainstorm.

🧠 Putting AI to the Test: Global Air & Ocean Movement

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.7.3 – Recognize how global patterns such as the jet stream and ocean currents influence local weather in measurable terms such as temperature and precipitation.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will use an AI image generator to create a scientific diagram that explains how global air or ocean patterns move heat around Earth and influence weather.

 

Scientists often use computer models, satellite images, and digital simulations to study large-scale Earth systems. These systems are too large to observe all at once, so visual models help scientists understand how heat and energy move across the planet.

 

Two of the most important global patterns are the jet stream and ocean currents.

 

The jet stream is a fast-moving river of air high in the atmosphere that helps steer storms and separate warm and cold air masses. It flows from west to east and can shift north or south, influencing weather patterns across continents.

 

Ocean currents are large streams of moving water in Earth’s oceans. These currents move heat from warm areas near the equator toward cooler regions near the poles. Warm currents increase air temperature and moisture, while cold currents lower temperatures and reduce moisture.

 

Both of these systems help move heat around the planet and influence weather in locations far from where the movement begins.

 

In this assignment, you will use an AI tool to generate an image that models one of these global patterns and then explain the science behind it.

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Identify global air and ocean patterns
• Explain how heat moves through Earth’s systems
• Describe how global patterns influence weather in different locations
• Interpret and analyze a scientific diagram

🌌 Mission Briefing

Meteorologists and climate scientists study global patterns to understand how weather systems move around Earth.

 

High above the planet, the jet stream flows quickly through the atmosphere, guiding storms and separating warm and cold air masses.

 

Meanwhile, powerful ocean currents move heat through Earth’s oceans, influencing coastal climates and helping balance Earth’s temperature.

 

These systems work together to move energy around the planet, helping explain why weather changes from place to place.

 

Your mission is to put AI to the test by using it as a scientific tool. You will generate a visual model showing how one of these global patterns moves heat and influences weather, then evaluate how well the AI represented the science.

🧰 Your Task

You will use an AI image generator to create a scientific diagram showing either the jet stream or ocean currents.

 

You may use any AI image generator, including:

• Canva Magic Media
• ChatGPT image generator
• Grok
• Another AI tool of your choice

 

Your generated image should visually show how air or water moves around Earth.

 

After generating the image, you will add labels and write a short scientific explanation describing how the system influences weather.

Step 1 — Choose a Global Pattern

Select ONE system to model:

• The Jet Stream
or
• Ocean Currents

 

Your image should show how heat or energy moves through that system.

Step 2 — Write Your AI Prompt

Before generating your image, write a clear prompt describing the scientific diagram you want the AI to create.

 

Your prompt should include:

• Earth or a world map
• Arrows showing movement of air or water
• Warm vs. cold regions
• An educational science diagram style

 

Example prompts:

Jet Stream Example:
“Educational science diagram of Earth showing the jet stream moving west to east across North America, arrows showing fast wind movement in the upper atmosphere separating warm and cold air masses.”

 

Ocean Current Example:
“World map showing ocean currents moving heat around the planet, warm currents shown in red and cold currents shown in blue with arrows showing water movement across the oceans.”

 

Generate 2–3 images and choose the one that best represents the science.

 

⚠️ Important: The example prompts above are only examples to help you understand how prompts work.

You may NOT copy or use my prompt for your image.

 

You must create your own prompt using your own wording.

 

AI tools often generate very similar images when the same prompt is used, which makes it easy to identify when prompts are copied. If the same prompt is used, the images will look nearly identical and it will be clear that the example prompt was used.

 

Your goal is to construct your own prompt like a scientist giving instructions to a computer model.

Step 3 — Add Scientific Labels

Download your image and add at least four science labels.

 

Examples of labels include:

• Jet Stream
• Atmosphere
• Warm Air
• Cold Air
• Ocean Current
• Warm Current
• Cold Current
• Heat Movement

 

You may add labels using Canva, Google Slides, PowerPoint, or another drawing tool.

Step 4 — Explain the Science

Write 4–6 sentences explaining:

• Which global pattern your diagram shows
• How heat moves through the system
• How this pattern can influence weather in another location

 

Your explanation should clearly connect the movement of air or water to changes in weather.

 

Be sure to spell check your writing and use proper grammar, capitalization, and punctuation before submitting.

🧠 Reflection Writing

Scientists often evaluate the tools they use to make sure the results are accurate. In this section, you will reflect on your experience using AI to create your scientific diagram.

 

Write a 4–6 sentence reflection explaining:

• Which AI tool you used
• Whether the AI image correctly showed the science

• Something the AI did incorrectly or something you had to fix

 

You must also include your final AI prompt in this section so your teacher can see how you guided the AI to create your image.

 

Your reflection and prompt may be:

• Typed in a Google Doc or Word document

 

Remember to spell check your writing and use proper grammar, capitalization, and punctuation before submitting.

✔ A 4–6 sentence reflection about using AI
✔ Your final AI prompt included with your reflection (notebook or typed document)

📹 Submission Requirement

Make sure your diagram clearly shows movement and scientific labels.

🦸‍♂️ When the Atmosphere Awakens:
An OPTIMA Science Comic Special Issue

 

📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.7.5 – “Explain how energy from the Sun influences global patterns of atmospheric movement and the temperature differences among air, water, and land.”

🎯 Objective
Independently create a science comic that explains how solar energy drives atmospheric movement on Earth.

 

Students will demonstrate understanding of how energy from the Sun causes air to move by accurately modeling the process, using correct scientific vocabulary, and clearly showing cause-and-effect relationships through visual storytelling.

 

Through this assignment, students will trace the flow of energy from the Sun to Earth’s surface and explain how uneven heating leads to temperature differences among land, water, and air. Students will then show how these temperature differences cause changes in air density, resulting in rising and sinking air, convection currents, and atmospheric movement.

 

By the end of this assignment, students should be able to visually and scientifically explain how energy from the Sun is directly connected to wind and large-scale patterns in Earth’s atmosphere.

🌌 Mission Briefing
At first glance, the air around us may seem still, calm, and invisible.

 

But in reality… it is constantly moving.

 

Every second of every day, energy from the Sun is striking Earth’s surface. This energy travels as radiation and is absorbed by land, water, and the atmosphere. As this energy spreads across the planet, it does not heat everything evenly.

 

Some areas receive more direct sunlight and become warmer, while other areas receive less direct sunlight and remain cooler. In addition, land, water, and air absorb and release energy at different rates. Land heats and cools quickly, while water changes temperature more slowly. These differences create even more variation in temperature across Earth.

 

These temperature differences are what set the atmosphere into motion.

 

When air is heated, it becomes less dense and rises upward. As it rises, cooler, more dense air moves in to take its place. This cooler air then warms and rises as well. This continuous cycle creates convection currents—circular patterns of moving air that drive wind and large-scale atmospheric movement across the planet.

 

This means that every breeze, gust of wind, and major weather system can be traced back to one powerful source:

 

The Sun.

 

Your mission is to transform this invisible process into a visual story.

 

You are not just drawing a comic—you are modeling a scientific system and showing how energy leads to motion across Earth.

⚠️ Comic Focus: Read Carefully

This comic is a little different than the other comic editions we have created this year.

 

In this assignment, your focus is not just on storytelling—it is on the science behind what is happening.

 

You are using the comic book / graphic novel format as a tool to explain a scientific process step-by-step.

 

Each panel should build on the previous one and clearly show how energy from the Sun leads to atmospheric movement.

 

Your mission is to transform this invisible process into a visual explanation.

 

You are not just drawing a comic—you are modeling a scientific system and showing how energy leads to motion across Earth.

🧰 Step 1: Comic Focus

Your comic must be a Scientific Breakdown.

🔬 Scientific Breakdown
Create a step-by-step science comic that explains the process in a clear, logical sequence. Your comic should feel like a visual explanation where each panel builds on the previous one.

 

Your goal is to clearly show how energy from the Sun leads to atmospheric movement on Earth.

 

Each panel should represent one part of the process and connect to the next to form a complete chain of events.

✏️ Step 2: Comic Requirements

Your comic must be:

✅ ONE full page
✅ Minimum of 6 panels
✅ Created by hand OR using AI tools

 

Each panel should represent part of the scientific process and connect clearly to the next. Your comic should read in a logical order and show a clear progression from solar energy reaching Earth to atmospheric movement forming.

🤖 AI Comic Expectations (Important)

If you choose to use AI to create your comic visuals, you are still responsible for the science, explanations, and accuracy of your work.

 

AI tools may help generate images, but they often create:

• Incorrect labels
• Misspelled or unreadable text
• Random or “gibberish” words
• Scientifically inaccurate visuals

 

Because of this:

👉 You MUST make corrections and add your own captions, labels, and explanations
👉 You MUST check all AI-generated content for accuracy
👉 You MUST ensure all words are clear, readable, and scientifically correct

 

Your grade is based on your understanding of the science, not the AI images.

 

⚠️ If your comic includes:
• Gibberish or unreadable words
• Incorrect vocabulary
• Missing or unclear explanations

 

➡️ It will lose points under Science Accuracy and Clarity

 

🧠 Remember:
AI is a tool — not the scientist.


YOU are responsible for explaining how energy from the Sun leads to atmospheric movement.

📖 Step 3: What Your Comic MUST Explain

Your comic must include ALL of the following scientific ideas:

1. ☀️ Solar Energy (Radiation)
Energy from the Sun traveling to Earth and being absorbed by the surface.

 

2. 🌍 Uneven Heating
Different parts of Earth heating at different rates due to sunlight angle and differences between land and water.

 

3. 🌡️ Temperature Differences
Uneven heating creating areas of warmer and cooler air.

 

4. 💨 Air Movement (Density)
Warm air rising because it is less dense and cool air sinking because it is more dense.

 

5. 🔄 Convection Currents
The continuous cycle of rising and sinking air.

 

6. 🌪️ Atmospheric Movement
Wind or large-scale movement of air across Earth.

📚 Step 4: Required Vocabulary

Solar energy
Radiation

Temperature

Convection currents
Atmospheric movement

 

👉 Vocabulary must be used correctly and in context to count.

🧠 Important Reminder

Your artistic style may vary—but the science expectations do not.

 

Every comic must clearly show that:

  • Energy from the Sun causes uneven heating
  • Uneven heating creates temperature differences among land, water, and air
  • Temperature differences cause air to move
  • Air movement forms convection currents
  • Convection currents drive atmospheric movement across Earth

 

Your comic should clearly show this chain of events from beginning to end.

In this assignment, you will step into the role of a scientist and design a Florida coastline in VR to investigate how natural disasters impact human life.

Florida’s location and environment make it especially vulnerable to natural disasters such as hurricanes, flooding, wildfires, and sinkholes.

 

These disasters can:
• Damage homes and buildings
• Cause flooding and environmental changes
• Force people to evacuate
• Disrupt communities and daily life

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Identify natural disasters that impact Florida
• Explain how these disasters affect people
• Show how communities prepare for and respond to disasters
• Design a model that represents a real-world situation

🌊⚠️ Mission Briefing

The lab lights flicker.

 

A warning alarm pulses across your workstation.

“Coastal Monitoring Systems… do you copy…”

 

The signal stabilizes as a live feed appears above your table.

Florida’s coastline comes into view—calm for a moment.

Then the data begins to change.

 

Water temperatures rise. Pressure drops. Winds begin to spiral.

A storm system rapidly intensifies over the Gulf of America.

 

Another alert overrides the feed:

“Impact zones forming. Coastal communities at risk.”

Satellite images update in real time—floodwaters pushing inland, roads disappearing, homes in the direct path of destruction.

 

A second transmission comes through, more urgent:

Scientists are struggling to model how these disasters affect people and communities. Without clear models:

• Damage cannot be predicted
• Evacuation plans cannot be improved
• Communities cannot prepare effectively

 

They need a way to visualize what is happening—and what will happen next.

 

You have been selected as part of the Florida Coastal Impact Team.

Your mission is to design a tabletop lab model of a Florida coastline and simulate how a natural disaster impacts the area and the people who live there.

 

Every part of your model must show what is happening, how it affects people, and what can be done to stay safe.

 

The alert fades.

The coastline map remains.

Your workstation is ready.

🎢 Extreme Earth: Designing an Educational Theme Park Experience
📜 Standard:
SC.6.E.7.8 – Differentiate among the various forms of severe weather conditions and describe how humans protect themselves from hazardous weather and sun exposure.

🎯 Objective

In this assignment, you will step into the role of a designer and create your own educational theme park based on how humans protect themselves from hazardous weather, natural disasters, and sun exposure.

 

Weather and sunlight are part of everyday life, but they can sometimes become dangerous. People must understand how to stay safe during events like hurricanes, flooding, wildfires, sinkholes, and other hazardous conditions.

 

Because hazardous conditions can impact people in different ways:

• Hurricanes can bring strong winds, heavy rain, and storm surge
• Flooding can quickly cover land and create dangerous conditions
• Wildfires can spread rapidly and threaten homes and ecosystems
• Sinkholes can form suddenly and damage land and structures
• Tornadoes can cause extreme destruction in a short amount of time
• Sun exposure can cause damage to skin and eyes

 

By the end of this assignment, you should be able to:

• Explain different types of hazardous weather and natural disasters
• Describe how humans protect themselves in different situations
• Connect science to real-world safety strategies
• Communicate ideas clearly through writing

🌦️ Mission Briefing

As visitors enter your theme park, they step into a world where conditions can change quickly and safety becomes the most important mission. From the moment they arrive, they are surrounded by experiences that show how powerful natural disasters and weather events can be, and how people respond to stay safe.

 

This is not just an amusement park—it is a place where every ride, attraction, and detail is intentionally designed to teach something meaningful. Guests are not only there for excitement, but to understand how humans prepare for and protect themselves from hurricanes, flooding, wildfires, sinkholes, and other hazardous conditions.

 

Throughout the park, visitors explore real-world scenarios. They experience what it feels like to prepare for a hurricane, respond to rising floodwaters, understand the dangers of wildfires, and learn how sinkholes can impact the land. They also see how people stay safe during extreme weather events like tornadoes and how to protect themselves from harmful sun exposure. Each attraction helps them understand the decisions people make to stay safe and why those choices matter.

 

However, this park is still in development, and the design team is looking for new ideas that bring learning and creativity together.

 

You have been selected as part of the Extreme Earth Design Team, and your role is to design a section of the park that is both engaging and educational. Your goal is to create an experience where visitors not only have fun, but leave with a deeper understanding of how humans protect themselves from hazardous weather, natural disasters, and sun exposure.

🧰 Your Task

You will write a minimum of 3 paragraphs explaining your educational theme park.

 

Your response MUST include:

  • The name of your theme park (and how/why it got its name)
  • A description of the overall theme and purpose for your park
  • Your top 2 rides or experiences at the park (Make sure you explain what type of ride or experience they are, what they teach the public, what colors the ride is... try to give me so many details I can picture it!)
  • How your park educates the public about hazardous weather, natural disasters, and sun exposure
  • A description of creative food and drink options in your park
  • How your park helps people understand how to stay safe during dangerous conditions

 

Your writing should clearly explain how your park connects to what we learned this week.

💡 Writing Expectations

• Minimum of 3 paragraphs
• You may write more if you choose
• Use clear explanations and creative details
• Stay focused on the topic
• Make connections to real-world science
• Use proper spelling, grammar, and complete sentences

🧾 Submission Options

You may choose what works best for you:

• Handwrite in your science notebook
• Type and submit as a Word or Google Doc

🚨 Important Note

Comments on the assignment will NOT be counted for a grade.

Make sure your work is submitted properly.

⭐ Bonus Opportunity

Want to take your theme park to the next level?

You can earn +2 bonus points by creating a logo for your theme park.

 

Your logo should:

• Match the theme and name of your park
• Be creative and visually clear
• Represent the purpose of your park

 

You may choose how to create your logo:

• ✏️ Hand-drawn in your notebook
• 💻 Digitally created (Canva, Google Slides, etc.)
• 🤖 AI-generated (if you use AI, include your prompt)

 

💡 If you use AI, make sure your prompt clearly describes your theme park and design ideas.

📊 Rubric

Creativity & Theme Park Design 5 Unique, engaging, and well-developed ideas

⭐ Bonus: Theme Park Logo +2 Creative logo that matches the park’s theme and purpose
